blocks.p: There was a line on the floor of Gin's genkan where August stopped.

It ran from wall to wall, a hand's width inside the door, exactly where the step up into the flat began. On one side of it was the wet heat of Obon week and the cicadas grinding away through the open window. On the other side was cold. It was not the cold of a draught. It was like the cold at the bottom of a well in summer. It felt old, like air that had been shut in a room for years.

blocks.cap: Iwata Shūji, the building's handyman, at work in the flat
Iwata Shūji, the building handyman, with his toolbox

blocks.p: Iwata Shūji was the handyman for the building. He had fixed forty-one doors in it over nineteen years, and he told Rei so before he told him anything else. He wanted it understood from the start that he was not a man who believed in things. He knelt in the genkan of Gin's flat with his toolbox open and his reading glasses pushed down his nose, and he talked the whole time. He talked the way some men talk when they are afraid of the quiet, building a wall of words against it.

Rei knew how to read that cold without having to think about it. It was the first thing in a Grid flyer Gin had folded into Chapter Three. Temperature is the first indicator. Not physical temperature, veil temperature. Veil cold did not spread the way real cold spreads. It sat in one place and pointed. The second sign was density, the heaviness of air before a storm that never came. The third was sound, which was not a sound at all, but the feeling that the silence had weight and was listening back. Gin had added a fourth sign in his own hand. Familiarity. The threat that feels like home. Rei stood on the warm side of the line and felt all four at once, in the doorway he had walked through every day of his life.

“It started after Obon began,” Iwata said, not looking at him. He was working a screwdriver he didn't need into a screw that didn't need it. “The tenant downstairs said her ceiling sweated. I came up to check the seal on the window. There's no leak. There's nothing. But you stand here...” He tapped the doorstep with the screwdriver, twice, on the exact line where the cold began. “...and you'll feel the building think you're a stranger.”

He laughed at his own words, and the laugh came out thin. Rei was standing in his brother's home, in the empty place where Gin's coat used to hang, and the cold was reading him. It was feeling for him in the dark and deciding what he was. Iwata had described it exactly. Rei understood that with a flat, quiet feeling that was worse than fear.
He knew what to do when something read him. He had known since before he could read.

blocks.cap: Gin at fourteen teaching small Rei to breathe at the kitchen table

blocks.p: He was five, maybe six, and it was this kitchen. The table had been too high, so Gin had put him on a cushion. Gin was fourteen and very serious. He made Rei breathe out slowly and then let his attention go loose, like letting a balloon string slip through his fingers. Not gone. Just loose. “Like you're bored,” Gin had said. “Like you're thinking about lunch.” They practised it every evening for a year, the way other children practised times tables. If anyone ever made the air feel funny, Gin said, that was what Rei should do. He should not hold his breath. He should not go still and careful. He should go a little bit stupid, on purpose, and stay that way until the funny feeling went away.
“Why?” Rei had asked.

“Because the wrong breath at the wrong moment marks you,” Gin had said. Then, because Rei was six and looked frightened, he had ruffled his hair and given him the version a child could carry. “Stay sloppy, Rei. Stay unremarkable. That's the whole trick.”

Rei had stayed sloppy for thirteen years. It was the skill he had practised most in his life. He had always thought it was just who he was. A well-liked, unfocused, ordinary boy. The intern who filed paper and forgot his umbrella.

Now he did it again, in the doorway, with the cold pressing on him. He breathed out. He let his attention go loose and a little foolish. He thought on purpose about whether there was any rice left in the freezer. He did not tighten. The cold passed over him the way a hand passes over a table in the dark, looking for something. It found a slightly bored young man thinking about lunch, and it moved on.
Iwata had noticed nothing. He was still talking.
Rei asked him, carefully, when he had last seen Gin. Iwata thought about it for longer than the question should have needed.

“That's the thing,” he said. “I saw him on the Sunday. Said good morning on the stairs. Polite man, your brother. Always was.” He set the screwdriver down. “But the missus in 3C, she swears she saw him on Friday, by the door, fitting his key. And I checked the log. He hasn't badged the front entrance since the Wednesday. So one of us is wrong about a man we both know on sight.”

He said it like a small mistake in the accounts. He did not hear yet what he had said. The building had been letting in someone who looked like Gin, on days Gin was not here, through a door that had started to make its own decisions.

He showed Rei the lock, because the lock was the reason he had been called, and a lock was something he could hold. Gin's key, the one Rei had picked up cold off the walkway at four in the morning, slid halfway into the lock and stopped.

Iwata took it from him and tried it himself. Gently, then less gently. His craftsman's patience turned slowly into the small insult a tradesman feels when a thing he understands refuses to behave. “This is his key,” he said. “I cut the spare myself, three years ago. It fit yesterday. I oiled it yesterday.” He drew it out and held the teeth up to the light, and found nothing wrong with them. The fault was not in the key. The fault was in the lock. Sometime between yesterday and now, it had quietly become a lock for a different door.
Then he showed Rei the other thing. It was the thing he had not wanted to call about, and had called about anyway. He pulled the door shut from the inside and let go.

The deadbolt turned. By itself. There was no hand on it, and no draught strong enough to move it. The bolt turned its full quarter-turn and slid home with a heavy, satisfied chunk. The flat had locked them both in.

Iwata stared at the brass knob as if it had spoken to him in a language he half remembered from childhood. For a long moment neither of them reached for it. Reaching for it meant admitting that something in the room had wanted the door shut, and had got its wish.

“It does that now,” Iwata said, very quietly. The wall of words was finally down. “Three times since Thursday. It locks itself. Like it's keeping something in. Or...” He could not stop the next part. It came out of him sideways. “...like it forgot which side the inside is on.”

Rei turned the bolt back. It came easily, oiled and ordinary, a thing a man had built and a man could undo. But he had felt it now, the small will in the room. The flat was no longer just a place his brother was missing from. It was taking part. The cold by the genkan, the changed lock and the bolt that locked itself were not three separate faults. They were one fact, told three ways, by a home that had started to speak.

Years ago, in the voice Rei had always trusted most, Gin had told him that a place holds the shape of whoever lives there, the way a glove holds the shape of a hand. This place was holding a shape. It was just not his brother's any more.

Iwata packed his toolbox slowly and carefully, with a kind of ceremony he would never have admitted to. At the door he stopped. He opened it now with his own master key, because Gin's key no longer worked and he would not say so out loud again. Then he gave Rei the thing he had been circling for an hour.

“My grandmother kept the house in Niigata,” he said. “She used to say a house knows when the owner's debt comes due. She said the cold spot was the house making room.” He shook his head at himself, ashamed to repeat it. He was a man who fixed things, repeating a thing that could not be fixed. “Making room for what, I asked her. She never said. I think she didn't like the answer either.”

Then he was gone down the stairs. Rei was alone in the doorway of his brother's flat in the high heat of Obon, the week when the line between the living and the dead is thinnest and the dead come home across the water. And the lock had been changed for whatever was coming across.

Outside, the afternoon went on as if nothing were wrong. The walkway was bright and hot, and the concrete smelled of dust and of the water someone had splashed on it to cool it down. From an open window on the floor below came the sound of a television showing the national high school baseball tournament, which every August fills the afternoons of the whole country. A bat cracked. A crowd cheered in a stadium far away in the west. From another flat came the smell of incense, burning on a family altar for the dead who were on their way home. Two doors down, the neighbour's futon still hung over the rail.

He did not go inside. He sat down on the warm side of the cold line, with his back against the wall of the outside walkway, and opened the archive on his knees at the place he had reached in order. It was the end of Chapter Four, the section on suppression. The heading said Read it twice. Nobody knows this exists. This is why high-rank practitioners die. Halfway down the page, Gin had stopped writing as a field officer and started writing to him.

blocks.cap: Suppression, a gift held below the surface

doc.title: Suppression. Technical reference, with Gin's notes
lines: What it is. A rare secondary ability allowing a practitioner to mask their true rank from external assessment, including Auditor reading, entity perception, and most detection equipment. The rank remains. The broadcast changes.

What it is not. A stability technique. A suppressed practitioner at 12% is still at 12%, presenting differently, at the same risk. Nor does it hide the structural thinning a high-rank aperture produces. It hides the signal. It cannot hide the effect.

Family lineage. Appears in family lines more strongly than any other secondary ability. The Uedera family variant produces an environmental interference pattern: the absence reads as background noise, not deliberate masking.

Rei Uedera. Presented rank: D. Null-signature reads as distracted, unfocused, a Sensitive rank not paying attention. This is the Uedera suppression variant functioning as trained. The disguise is working.
Actual rank: A. Possibly touching S at ceiling.

To Rei, if this is you: your null reads as distraction. Do not tighten it. The slightly sloppy, slightly unfocused quality is the disguise and it works because it is consistent. The day you present a clean null it will read as deliberate masking and someone will start asking why. Stay sloppy. Stay unremarkable. Read Chapter 5 twice. Then read it again.

blocks.p: Rei read the page once, then again, slowly, until he was sure what it said. Suppression was a way of hiding how much power a person had. The power stayed the same. Only what other people could feel of it changed. In the Uedera family it worked in a particular way. It did not make a person feel empty, which would look suspicious. It made them feel like noise, like someone not paying attention. That was what Gin had taught him at the kitchen table. And everyone who had ever looked at Rei had felt a D, a low and harmless grade. Under the noise, the page said, he was an A.

Rei looked at the single letter and did not feel anything for a while. He did not know yet exactly where an A sat on the Division's scale. He knew that his brother, after six years, was officially a C. He had always been the boy who was bad at exams and good at noticing, who fell asleep on the couch in the afternoons and never knew why he was so tired. Gin had known why. Gin had written it down in a book, put the book on a shelf and made him rice. Rei turned the pages forward through Chapter Five and Chapter Six, faster than Gin would have liked, until he found the note Gin had put at the very end of the addendum, on its own page.

doc.title: Personal Archive. Private Note
lines: I have been debating including this since I began the archive. Including it now.
The family has never passed information about this. My parents did not know what they were carrying.

What I know about my ancestors is from their case files. Two of them were field operatives during the early period, before the CVD's current structure existed, when a specific unit was deployed to manage what was crossing over from the other side. In those files there are moments where the documented response should not have been possible for a single-path practitioner at the recorded rank.

They had blocked one path each, maybe two. Not unlocked, blocked, held unused alongside whatever they presented as. The same way I present as C and hold the rest back. They never opened what they had. They just held it there, and occasionally, under sufficient pressure, something else moved.

I have unlocked four paths. Not fully. But they are present and accessible and when I push hard enough in the right direction they engage. I have been developing it deliberately for four years without telling anyone, because the ability taxonomy from the CVD does not have a category for what I am describing.

Rei. I believe he has the same profile. The way his Clairsentience bleeds into other registers occasionally in ways that a single-path ability should not. The specific chaos of his passive output, which reads as multiple things interfering with each other rather than one thing running loud. I believe he has more than one path available to him. I believe he has not accessed any of them deliberately.

I have not told him this. I am going to have the conversation. I am documenting this commitment here, again, in the hope that committing it to the archive creates the accountability I have not been able to create through internal resolve alone.
Keys on the hook. Said something I have not said before. The archive is more complete than it was this morning.

blocks.p: A path, Rei knew from the earlier chapters, was the kind of power a person had. Reading what people and places give off was one path. Moving things without touching them was another. Most people with power had one path, and only one, for their whole life.

So that was the secret. It was not a curse. It was not a superpower. It was a family of people born with more than one door open, who had learned, one generation after another, to stand in front of the extra doors so nobody would see them. Rei had been born with two. He could feel the second one now that he knew to look, the way a person suddenly notices a sound that has been in the room all along. It was nothing he could name. It was only the sense that the noise Gin had taught him to make had always been covering more than one thing.
Gin had been going to tell him. He had written that down twice, in two different chapters, and then he had run out of time.

Rei thought about the entries in the archive that stopped being entries after the fourteenth. He thought about the case Gin had closed too fast, the drowning, and the address in no file. He thought about a debt that had never been Gin's to pay, and the brother who would pay it anyway, with the only thing he had left, which was his own place in his own life.

And he understood, sitting there, that this was what it looked like from the outside. Not a disappearance. Not violence. Nothing the Division had a form for. A change of tenant. A man slowly handing himself over to whatever he had agreed to let in. And the only witnesses were a handyman who did not believe in things and a brother who was learning, room by room, to read the signs before he could bear to say what they meant.

He took the key, Gin's useless key that fit nothing now, and put it in his pocket anyway. It was the shape of a door Gin had once been able to open. Rei was not ready to be a man who threw away the last key to his brother.

Behind him, as he pulled the door shut from the warm side, the deadbolt turned. He did not reach for it. He let the flat keep what it was keeping. He went down the stairs into the heat, and the cicadas took him back. He carried the cold out into August in the small of his back, where it would sit for days, reading him, deciding what he was. And every time it looked, it would find a slightly bored young man, thinking about lunch.
